raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with rashes on her left cheek and chest. Initially, a rash developed on the left cheek three months prior, with no obvious inducing factor and the patient gradually developed a similar rash on her left chest, and the area gradually increased. The rash did not cause any symptoms such as itching, irritation, or pain. Little improvement was noted after one month of external treatment with tacrolimus and halometasone creams, but the patient developed occasional tenderness.
The patient was in good health and denied any history of chronic disease, drug allergies, or genetic diseases. Physical examination revealed no obvious abnormalities in the heart, lung, or abdomen, and no swelling of any superficial lymph nodes in the body.
Clustered yellow papules (diameter 5 mm) with clear boundaries were found on the left cheek, covering an area of approximately 3 cm x 3 cm. The surface was smooth and had a waxy luster (Figure 1A). A similar rash was seen on the left chest, covering an area of approximately 6 cm x 3.5 cm with a clear boundary, smooth surface, waxy luster, mild infiltration and hypertrophy, normal skin temperature, and no tenderness (Figure 1B). Some of the papules were fused and varied in color (red, brown, deep red).
Blood test revealed that the total immunoglobulin E (IgE) level was 389.0 kU/L; the level of ferritin, a tumor biomarker, was below average at 9.70 microg/L. Blood analysis demonstrated negative results for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis and AIDS. Blood glucose levels were normal. High-resolution chest CT showed mild chronic inflammation in the left lung, multiple small lymph nodes in the mediastinum, and flocculent shadows in the anterior mediastinum in the region of the thymus. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a hepatic cyst. Histopathological examination of the left chest skin lesion showed a roughly normal epidermis with cell masses in the dermis. The phagocytic histiocytes had deep irregular nuclei with pale and frothy cytoplasm. Lymphocytes, plasma cells, a small number of neutrophils and eosinophils were observed in the mass upon hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining (Figure 2). Emperipolesis phenomenon was also observed (Figure 3). IHC staining showed S100 (+) (Figure 4A), CD68 (+) (Figure 4B), and CD1a (-) (Figure 4C).
After relevant auxiliary examinations and whole-body physical and hematological examinations, it was confirmed that the patient had no lymph node enlargement or visceral involvement. Thus, the diagnosis of primary papulonodular-type CRDD was made.
No treatment was initiated and the skin lesions partially disappeared three months after diagnosis (Figure 5A and B). The patient is still being monitored via follow-up examinations (Figure 6).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of asymptomatic clustered waxy yellow-to-reddish-brown papules and plaques on her left cheek and left anterior chest.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months prior to presentation, the patient developed a painless, non-pruritic papular plaque on her left cheek without an identifiable trigger, followed by a larger similar plaque on her left chest. One month of topical tacrolimus and halometasone creams yielded minimal improvement with occasional mild tenderness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no chronic systemic diseases, genetic disorders, or drug allergies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left cheek and left chest papulonodular plaques with occasional mild tenderness; negative for pruritus, fever, or systemic symptoms. Recent medications: topical tacrolimus and halometasone creams.

objective.physical_examination: Cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and superficial lymph node examinations were normal. Dermatological examination revealed a 3 x 3 cm cluster of well-demarcated 5-mm smooth, waxy yellow papules on the left cheek, and a 6 x 3.5 cm well-demarcated, mildly infiltrated plaque of coalescent red, brown, and yellow waxy papules on the left chest.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests showed elevated total serum IgE (389.0 kU/L), low serum ferritin (9.70 ug/L), normal blood glucose, and negative serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C. High-resolution chest CT showed mild chronic left lung inflammation, small mediastinal nodes, and anterior mediastinal thymic remnants; abdominal ultrasound showed a benign hepatic cyst.
objective.advanced_workup: Left chest skin biopsy histopathology demonstrated a normal epidermis overlying dermal sheets of large phagocytic histiocytes with pale, foamy cytoplasm and irregular nuclei exhibiting prominent emperipolesis (intact lymphocytes engulfed within histiocyte cytoplasm), admixed with lymphocytes, plasma cells, neutrophils, and eosinophils. Immunohistochemistry was positive for S100 and CD68 and negative for CD1a.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed primary papulonodular cutaneous Rosai-Dorfman disease (CRDD; secondary/nodular syphilis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and systemic RDD excluded via negative syphilis serology, negative CD1a, positive S100/CD68 emperipolesis, and absence of nodal/visceral involvement). Managed with clinical observation alone without systemic therapy, achieving spontaneous partial regression of the cheek and chest lesions at 3-month follow-up.
